title: The Leaked Signing Key
role: You are the engineer responsible for your company's software signing.
objective: Recover from a leaked code-signing key without breaking customer trust.
environment: A private signing key was committed to a public repository six days ago. Customers verify your software updates against the matching public key.

state_variables.trust_intact: Customer trust in updates, starts at 100

stages.narrative: A scanner flags the key in a public repository. It has been there six days.

choices.text: Treat the key as compromised: start revoking and rotating it, and record when it was exposed.
choices.feedback: Correct. A key that has been public must be assumed copied. Rotation and revocation start immediately, and the exposure window defines which signatures need review.

choices.text: Delete the file in a new commit and force-push.
choices.feedback: The key is already in clones, forks, caches and the history others have seen. Deleting it removes nothing from an attacker's copy.

choices.text: Wait for the next scheduled release to rotate the key.
choices.feedback: Every day of delay is a day an attacker can sign malicious updates that customers will accept.

stages.narrative: Rotation is under way. You need to know which signatures are suspect.
stages.decision_prompt: How do you handle existing signed artefacts?

choices.text: Compare all artefacts signed since the exposure against your build records; re-sign genuine ones with the new key and flag any that have no record.
choices.feedback: Correct. Build records tell you what you really signed. Anything signed in the window without a record is suspicious.

choices.text: Assume only the most recent release is affected.
choices.feedback: The attacker could have signed anything during the whole exposure window. Without the comparison you cannot know.

choices.text: Invalidate everything ever signed, including years of releases, without review.
choices.feedback: It removes the risk but breaks every customer's installed software and update path for no reason; scope the action to the exposure window.

stages.narrative: Customers' tools trust the old public key.
stages.decision_prompt: How do you move customers to the new key safely?

choices.text: Publish a signed advisory and the new key fingerprint through an independent channel, revoke the old key, and run a defined transition period.
choices.feedback: Correct. Customers need a way to verify the new key that does not depend on the compromised one; an independent channel and a clear timetable give them that.

choices.text: Silently ship the new key in the next update.
choices.feedback: An update signed with the old key could be the attacker's. Customers cannot tell a genuine key change from a malicious one.

choices.text: Email customers the new key as an attachment.
choices.feedback: Email can be spoofed, which is exactly what an attacker would do. Use a channel the customer can authenticate.

stages.narrative: The incident is contained. How do you prevent a repeat?

choices.text: Add secret scanning to CI, move signing keys into an HSM or key-management service, use short-lived signing identities, and review who has access.
choices.feedback: Correct. Keys that never leave an HSM cannot be committed, short lifetimes limit damage, and scanning catches mistakes early.

choices.text: Run a developer awareness session only.
choices.feedback: Training helps but a single slip still leaks a long-lived key. Controls should make the mistake impossible or harmless.

choices.text: Make the repository private and change nothing else.
choices.feedback: It hides the symptom. The key is still a long-lived file in source control and the old copies are still out there.

stages.narrative: The release manager reviews the incident outcome.

bands.title: Trust preserved
bands.text: SUCCESS. The key was revoked quickly, the exposure window audited, customers moved to the new key on an independent channel, and controls added.

bands.title: Partly recovered
bands.text: PARTIAL. The immediate danger is reduced, but forgery risk or customer trust remains weaker than it should be.

bands.title: Still exposed
bands.text: AT RISK. The key remains usable by an attacker or customers lost confidence in your updates.

resolution.concept_reveal: A leaked private key is compromised for good. The response is revoke, rotate, scope the damage by the exposure window, and tell relying parties through a channel they can authenticate. Prevention is structural: keys in HSMs or key-management services, short lifetimes, and automatic secret scanning (NIST SP 800-57 on key management).

replayability_note: Try the other options to see why each fails.
